notes:
Searching first.Below are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 55, using the sources I was able to read. Each note gives its page URL.

**Gaps:** I found nothing on this psalm from the Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican sites, from the NET Bible notes, from bibleodyssey.org, or from Orthodox sources. I also found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it. I only saw Augustine's exposition through search excerpts, not the full page. Where a verse is thin or missing below, that's why.

**Background (whole psalm)**
- Guzik: most commentators link the psalm to Absalom's rebellion, with Ahithophel as the friend who betrayed David. He adds that some parts don't fit, since it's hard to picture David wishing Absalom into Sheol (v. 15). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Guzik sees three stages in the psalm: fear (wanting to fly away like a dove), fury (asking God to divide the enemies' tongues), then faith (giving the burden to the Lord). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Gill: the setting was either Saul's persecution or Absalom's plot. He says many Christian teachers see Ahithophel as a picture of Judas, and that much of the psalm "may be truly applied to Christ." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html
- Matthew Henry disagrees on that last point. He grants that some read Ahithophel as a figure of Judas, but says nothing in the psalm is applied to Christ in the New Testament. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm
- A dissenting older view: Ellicott says the traditional link to David can't be kept up. In his reading the singer is being oppressed, not overthrown by a revolt. The friend may stand for a whole group of Israelites who turned traitor and sided with foreign oppressors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm

**v. 1**
- Spurgeon: the title means a song played with stringed instruments. He notes how naturally and constantly believers turn to prayer when in trouble. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps055.php
- Guzik: David felt that God was far away, as if hiding from him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Gill ties the plea to the covenant of grace. He also reads it of Christ praying "in the days of his flesh." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: the verb for "restless" is used elsewhere of a wanderer's roving life and of moral and political instability. "Moan" carries the sense of a sufferer who has to let out his groans. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Spurgeon: we may complain *to* God, though not *of* him. Even our rambling, distracted thoughts can be brought to him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm

**v. 3**
- Barnes: "voice" points to slander, meaning attacks on David's character that he couldn't answer. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-55.html
- Ellicott: "release disaster" is better translated "roll mischief." The picture is probably of rolling stones down on an enemy from higher ground. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Matthew Henry: they could find no wrong in David, so they piled every kind of wrong on him and painted him as a tyrant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: David's heart "writhes with pain." The "terrors of death" mean a horror of death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Barnes: the Septuagint, Vulgate and Luther translate it "fear of death." Barnes thinks it more natural to read it as pangs *like* the pangs of death. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-55.html
- Gill sees here Christ's sorrow in Gethsemane and on the cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html

**v. 5**
- Barnes: David had no way of knowing how far the rebellion had spread, and his life seemed to be at risk. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-55.html
- Gill links the "horror" to Christ being "sore amazed" in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). He says it came from bearing his people's sins and God's wrath in their place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/55-5.html

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew literally says "who will give me?" The bird is probably the rock pigeon, which nests on cliffs far from people. "Rest" is more literally "dwell." https://biblehub.com/psalms/55-6.htm
- Gill: the dove was chosen because it is harmless and its enemies are like hawks, and also because it flies fast. He notes that David did in fact flee from Absalom in haste (2 Samuel 15:14). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html
- Calvin: the words show how desperate David's situation was, so that exile looked like a blessing. They suggest he could only escape by a miracle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/55-6.html
- Spurgeon warns that the wish is vain, because inward grief goes wherever we go. It is cowardly to avoid a battle God wants us to fight. Like Noah's dove, which found rest only back in the ark, we can find rest in Jesus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm

**v. 7**
- Guzik: David may have been longing for his earlier wilderness years, when he had often seen God's faithfulness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Guzik quotes Maclaren: the wish stayed a wish, and David had to stay at his post. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- JFB: Jeremiah 9:2 echoes this verse. The dove is named less for speed than for being defenceless and innocent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-55.html

**v. 8**
- Gill: the "storm" is an army of rebels sweeping everything before it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html
- Matthew Henry: what David wanted from escaping was rest, not victory. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: many hear an echo of Babel here. He quotes Kidner, who says David is asking God to use the way evil naturally splits apart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Ellicott: "divide their tongues" means "cause division in their councils." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Matthew Henry: the prayer was answered when Hushai's advice overturned Ahithophel's (2 Samuel 17). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm
- Spurgeon: the rebels were soon split. Ahithophel hanged himself, and Absalom was left hanging in a tree. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: violence and strife are pictured as people walking the walls on patrol. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Gill notes Aben Ezra's picture of the city as a circle: violence and strife run round the edge, with mischief and sorrow at the centre. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: "streets" means the open squares by the gate, where public business and justice were done. The scene is one of bad government. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Spurgeon: smooth talkers in every public place were turning people against their good king. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm

**v. 12**
- Spurgeon: "None are such real enemies as false friends." He adds that we can put up with Shimei more easily than Ahithophel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm
- Barnes: a former friend's words do extra damage because people assume he speaks from inside knowledge. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-55.html

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew means a man of equal standing. The Septuagint and Vulgate have "of one soul with me." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Wesley: the man was David's equal in reputation and influence, not in power. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/55.htm
- Gill applies the verse to both Ahithophel and Judas. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/55-13.html

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: "walked with the crowd" refers to the great public processions to the temple. The two men's friendship was public as well as private. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Spurgeon says this was true of Ahithophel and, in a measure, of Judas. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm

**v. 15** (the curse in this verse is where commentators differ most)
- Guzik: it is a strong prayer, but it leaves vengeance to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Guzik also quotes Kidner, who hears an echo of Korah's rebels going down alive (Numbers 16:30). He quotes Boice, who notes that David does not curse the former friend by name. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Gill (Baptist): the curse comes from zeal for God's glory, not from revenge. It is a prophecy, not an example for ordinary Christians to copy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html
- Matthew Henry (Presbyterian) says much the same: we should treat such prayers as prophecies, not use them against our own personal enemies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm
- Spurgeon (Baptist) reads it either as a warrior's curse or as a confident prediction. He warns that a softness which treats punishment as cruelty is now a bigger danger than the harshness of earlier times. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm
- Coffman (Church of Christ) says there was no point in praying for the conversion of men like these. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-55.html
- Ellicott: the written Hebrew text reads "desolations upon them." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: David switches suddenly from cursing to calm confidence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Spurgeon: God's covenant name (LORD) is the pledge that he will keep his covenant promise. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm
- Coffman: David's confidence rested on God's promise to him in 2 Samuel 7:16. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-55.html

**v. 17**
- Gill: Jewish tradition traces the morning, afternoon and evening prayer times to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html
- Matthew Henry: praying three times a day was probably David's habit already. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm
- Spurgeon: David meets his enemies' constant activity with constant prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps055.cfm

**v. 18**
- Guzik: the battle went on, but David's soul was at peace. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Matthew Henry: if God did not give David victory, he gave him inward peace. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm
- Ellicott thinks the Hebrew text here is probably damaged. He prefers the Septuagint, "from those drawing near to me." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Augustine (Catholic, via search excerpts) reads "they were with me in many things" as heretics who share the sacraments but not love. They are chaff, not wheat. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801055.htm

**v. 19** ("they do not change" is unclear, and readings vary)
- Guzik: the phrase is obscure. It may mean they never change for the better, or that hard times have never forced them to change. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Guzik quotes Maclaren on Calvin's view: the "changes" are changes of fortune, so steady prosperity breeds forgetfulness of God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
- Wesley: they "meet with no crosses nor disappointments," so they carry on without any fear of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/55.htm
- Ellicott takes "no changes" as describing God, who never varies (compare James 1:17). He thinks the Selah is out of place. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Gill reports the same reading from the Jewish scholar Kimchi. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-55.html
- Augustine: the phrase means people who die still stubborn and divided from the church. They are never changed for the better. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801055.htm
- Barnes: God "inhabits antiquity." He is eternal and unchanging. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-55.html

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: the traitor is singled out again. "Violates" literally means "pierced," and he links this to an old practice of cancelling a bond by driving a nail through it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Gill: Ahithophel planned to strike the king alone (2 Samuel 17:1). Judas, in a similar way, gave the sign for Jesus' arrest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/55-20.html
- Coffman: Ahithophel knowingly went against God's will for David's kingdom. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-55.html

**v. 21**
- Ellicott suspects the Hebrew text is damaged here and suggests reading "smoother than butter is his face." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
- Matthew Henry: such men smile while they stab, like Joab, "that kissed and killed." Satan flatters people in the same way. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm
- Guzik: David showed honour by not naming the man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/

**v. 22**
- What "burden" means:
  - Ellicott: the word probably means "gift," and so a person's "lot." The Septuagint's "care" paved the way for 1 Peter 5:7. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/55.htm
  - Ellicott (on the verse page): God sustains us without necessarily taking the burden away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/55-22.htm
  - JFB: "sustain" literally means "supply food." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/55-22.htm
- What "never let the righteous be shaken" means (Calvinist and Arminian readers differ here):
  - Barnes (Presbyterian): God will not let the righteous "fall away and perish" for good. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/55-22.html
  - Gill (Calvinist Baptist): the righteous will not fall "totally and finally," and nothing can move them out of their state of grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/55-22.html
  - Wesley (Methodist): give God all your "crosses, and cares, and fears" by faith and prayer. He may let the righteous be shaken for a time, but not overwhelmed. Wesley does not cast this in terms of final perseverance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/55-22.html
  - Pulpit Commentary: the promises are only for the righteous who trust God fully. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/55-22.htm

**v. 23**
- Wesley: "not live out half their days" means they will die early and violently. "I will trust in You" means waiting quietly for deliverance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/psalms/55.htm
- Matthew Henry: men who cut others off will be cut short themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_055.cfm
- Coffman reads "the pit" as final, eternal condemnation. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-55.html
- Guzik: the psalm ends with David looking at God rather than at his enemies. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-55/
